title: Baptism and Communion
objective: After this level you can explain how Christians practice baptism and Communion and why churches understand them differently.
summary: Baptism with water admits a person to the church, as an infant or as a professing believer; Communion recalls the Last Supper, and churches differ on what happens to the bread and wine.

cards.headline: Water, bread and wine: Christianity's two great rituals.
cards.body: Churches practice both, and practice them differently. Who should be baptized? What happens to the bread? The answers show what each church believes.

cards.headline: Baptism: the way in
cards.body: Baptism is Christianity's rite of admission. Water is used, by full immersion, pouring or sprinkling, with the words "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit". Paul described it as sharing in Christ's death, burial and resurrection. Picture the full-immersion version: going under, coming back up.

cards.headline: Babies or believers?
cards.body: Most traditional churches, including Catholic, Lutheran, Anglican and Reformed, baptize infants. Baptists and some others baptize only people old enough to profess their faith themselves, a practice rooted in the Anabaptists of the Reformation. Both agree baptism starts a Christian life. They disagree on whether the person's own faith must come first.

cards.headline: Communion: a remembered meal
cards.body: The Eucharist, from the Greek for "thanksgiving", is also called Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper. It commemorates Jesus's Last Supper, when, the Gospels say, he blessed bread and wine and told his disciples to repeat it in his memory. For most churches it is the central act of worship.

cards.headline: What's in the cup?
cards.body: Here churches part ways. Catholics teach transubstantiation: the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood while still looking like bread and wine. Orthodox Christians affirm Christ's real presence in their own terms. Lutherans affirm a real presence too, but not transubstantiation. The Swiss reformer Zwingli saw a memorial, and some churches call it an ordinance rather than a sacrament.

cards.headline: Baptism and Communion: the takeaways
learned: Baptism admits a person to the church, as infant or believer
Churches differ on what happens to the bread and wine

questions.prompt: Which churches baptize only people old enough to profess their own faith?
questions.explanation: Baptists baptize professing believers, a practice rooted in the Anabaptists.

questions.prompt: Match each church or reformer with its teaching.
questions.explanation: Catholics teach transubstantiation, Zwingli saw the Eucharist as a memorial, and Baptists baptize only people old enough to profess their own faith.

questions.prompt: Baptism admits a person into the church, which in Level 7's terms makes it _____.

options.label: a canon of sacred texts
options.rationale: A canon is a collection of scriptures.

options.label: a creed recited in worship
options.rationale: A creed states beliefs; baptism changes a person's status.

questions.explanation: Like any rite of passage, baptism moves a person from one religious status to another: into the church.
